kaigo-atomic-accessible-talk.heading: Support conversation according to communication needs
paragraphs: To support communication, check which information the person finds difficult to receive and how they can most easily express wishes. Do not choose a method from a diagnosis or disability label alone. Ask about experience and preferences, and check whether the method actually works.

When approaching someone with limited sight, call their name first and introduce your name and role. Touching them silently may startle them. Describe shapes, features, direction and distance specifically rather than relying only on ‘here’ or ‘there.’

Agree with the person on the reference for directions. Use left and right from their viewpoint or an agreed sound direction rather than a reference only staff understand. If the person wishes and an object is safe to touch, touch can also help them check it.

Clock-position descriptions communicate an item’s direction by relating it to a clock face. Braille conveys written information; tactile paving provides cues for movement. Their purposes differ, and not everyone with limited sight reads Braille.

With someone who has difficulty hearing, speak from the front in as quiet a place as possible so they can see your face and mouth movements. Speak slowly and clearly at a volume suited to them, rather than shouting from the outset. If a better-hearing side has been established, consider that side together with visibility of your face.

Writing, text-display devices, lip-reading, sign language and hearing aids use different channels. Sign language combines hand and finger movements with facial expressions and movements of the head, neck and other areas to convey meaning. Check which language or method the person can use.

A hearing aid receives sound through a microphone, processes and amplifies it, and delivers it to the ear. Louder sound alone does not guarantee understanding of words. Check whether the actual message has been received, using writing, pictures or other methods too.

Difficulty hearing can make joining conversations harder, and some people experience loneliness or loss. Do not assume everyone feels the same. Ask about feelings and consider accessible participation and any necessary psychological support together.

With aphasia, understanding spoken language, speaking, reading and writing are not necessarily affected equally. Adapt short, clear sentences, pictures, gestures and easy-to-answer questions. Avoid interrupting the person to correct every small verbal mistake; check the meaning they want to convey. If safety-related information is unclear, confirm rather than guess.

When someone with dementia repeats a story or gives an account differing from facts, listen to their concerns and anxiety. Speak slowly using short phrases and check necessary facts. Avoid both trying to defeat them in an argument and affirming unconfirmed content as fact.

Handing over ICT or another device does not complete communication support. Check with the person whether they can operate it, understand content and express wishes. Consult the person responsible about uncertainties, and do not proceed with physical touch or method changes without the person’s consent.

Learning case: the person uses the wrong name for an item but points to what they want to use. Rather than making them wait until they say the name correctly, check the indicated item and their wishes. However, do not omit checks when safety-related use is unclear.

kaigo-atomic-record-handover.heading: Check the recipient’s understanding in records and handovers
paragraphs: Care plans, progress records, handover notebooks and meetings each help share information. Recording condition, support provided, personal responses and outcomes gives the next worker a basis for continuing care. Do not record support that was only planned as having been carried out.

Record as promptly as possible using the correct date and time. If the event time differs from the later recording time, distinguish them using the facility’s method. Do not fill gaps in uncertain memories as though they were confirmed facts.

The person’s words, feelings and wishes are subjective information. What workers observe and values actually measured are objective information. Examples include measured blood pressure and temperature and test data shared by healthcare professionals. Identify the source of test data; care workers do not use it to diagnose independently. Subjective information is not worthless, and numbers do not justify ignoring the person’s own words. Record sources separately.

Organize when, where, who was involved, what happened, how you responded and any known reasons. The 5W1H approach helps communicate information; it is not a set of blanks to fill with guessed causes. If the cause is unknown, say it remains unconfirmed.

Treat names, addresses, phone numbers and photographs as personal information. Follow facility procedures to check purpose, necessary scope, recipients, methods, personal consent or other appropriate grounds. Do not post personal or workplace matters on private social media or discuss them outside without authorization.

Senders separate observations from judgments and assumptions, and communicate key points briefly. Choose timing according to urgency; for ordinary consultations, also check that the location protects personal information from being overheard. Share workers’ own work situation or things noticed through contact with the person when needed for support.

Recipients also have more to do than listen. Note what is needed and repeat important points such as times, the person concerned, response, next responsible worker and unconfirmed matters. Silence or lack of objection does not prove understanding or acceptance of responsibility.

Making a call, the recipient receiving it, accepting the next task and actually completing a response are separate states. Do not record a problem as resolved merely because contact was made. Confirm who will next check what and how results will be communicated.

Consultation means seeking colleagues’ or professionals’ opinions and assistance about uncertainties or problems. Specify what you are unsure about and ask someone whose role fits. Wanting to finish quickly does not justify decisions outside your responsibilities.

For urgent changes or accidents, obtain help and make contact immediately rather than waiting to complete a form. This teaches records and information management; it does not independently establish workplace emergency procedures, legal grounds for sharing or medical judgments.

Learning case: the recipient remains silent after a report containing several times. Ask them to repeat key times, the person concerned, next actions and unconfirmed matters to check shared understanding. Do not record silence as agreement.

kaigo-atomic-continence-types.heading: Distinguish elimination aids and mechanisms of urinary leakage
paragraphs: A commode may be used when the person feels the need to urinate or defecate but cannot easily reach the toilet, or at night. Urinals and bedpans used in bed support people who have difficulty moving or sitting, among others. Knowing a purpose differs from being able to select and position suitable equipment. The source also illustrates in-bed equipment for physically weakened people and different urinal shapes labeled for men or women. Labels alone do not establish fit: check the body, posture and actual product.

Incontinence briefs and pads help manage urine or stool leakage and difficulty using a toilet. They do not replace checking causes, opportunities to use the toilet, personal initiative or skin observation. Check habits and necessary assistance. Some people also find commode use difficult, so consider methods individually according to condition.

Leakage when coughing, sneezing or otherwise increasing abdominal pressure describes stress urinary incontinence. Distinguish its mechanism from urge urinary incontinence, in which a sudden strong urge is followed by leakage before reaching the toilet. Do not interpret ‘urge’ here as merely psychological tension.

Other types include overflow urinary incontinence, where retained urine overflows in small amounts, and reflex leakage related to neurological impairment. Accurate reporting of leakage patterns matters, but those patterns alone do not allow care workers to establish a type or cause.

Functional urinary incontinence relates to difficulties reaching the toilet in time because of movement, clothing management or recognizing the toilet’s location. A person may feel the urge but be unable to find the toilet. Check routes, guidance, suitable timing and assistance; do not treat all leakage as having the same mechanism.

Constipation can relate to bodily functions or to obstructed passage from tumors, inflammation and other factors. Do not count days alone: compare with the person’s usual bowel pattern and record amounts, frequency, stool characteristics, distress and changes. Refer to healthcare professionals when assessment of the cause is needed.

Daily-life support for constipation may include opportunities following usual bowel habits, fluids and fiber consistent with the plan, and permitted activities. Report lack of improvement. Do not uniformly increase fluids or fiber without checking drinking restrictions, swallowing, illnesses or obstruction. This material also does not authorize independently increasing or reducing medication.

Diarrhea involves continuing watery stools and requires attention to dehydration and irritation of skin around the anus. Report new diarrhea and similar changes to healthcare professionals, including the possibility of infection. Follow facility methods to maintain cleanliness and skin condition so stool does not remain against the skin for long.

Check swallowing, underlying conditions, healthcare instructions and the plan to determine whether oral fluids are possible and which types and amounts are suitable. Examples of warm water or sports drinks are not instructions to give everyone the same amount. A comfortable drinking temperature alone does not prove suitability for the fluid replacement the person needs.

Listen to discomfort, embarrassment and anxiety about elimination without blame or teasing. Observe urine and stool and report health abnormalities according to urgency. Completed cleaning does not mean assessment of the person’s condition is complete. Psychological tension can affect elimination, so check difficulties in a way that makes them easier to discuss.

Learning case: the person felt the urge to urinate but could not find the toilet in time. Do not finish with changing the brief alone. Check guidance, mobility assistance, timing, skin and wishes. Leakage alone does not diagnose the cause.

kaigo-atomic-toilet-environment.heading: Support each elimination stage and a usable environment
paragraphs: Elimination involves several stages: noticing the need, reaching the location, arranging clothing and posture, eliminating, cleaning, restoring clothing and leaving the area. Identify the stage needing assistance and preserve parts the person can perform.

Easy-to-operate doors such as sliding doors, wheelchair approach space, usable grab bars and a reachable nurse-call button support toilet use. Also check odor, ventilation and privacy. Equipment being installed does not establish that this person can use it.

An L-shaped grab bar can support standing, while an adjustable grab bar can accommodate approach and physical condition. The call system requests help with difficulty or after finishing. Check with the person that it is reachable and operable in their actual posture. The source’s adjustable grab bar moves up and down. In practice, check product instructions and the person’s movements.

In a hemiplegia toileting example, the usable hand holds the grab bar while the helper supports stability on the weaker side. Before standing, separately check feet, clothing and the available handhold. Do not substitute pulling the affected arm to bring the person upright. The source example lowers trousers and underwear while the unaffected hand holds the bar and the affected side is supported, then uses the bar to sit on the toilet. Do not apply this sequence universally. Use an individual method after confirming that standing and transfer are possible.

Check sitting stability. Adjusting clothing while seated as far as the person can helps reduce tasks performed standing. If standing is possible and permitted, support it using the planned method. After standing, check stability and clothing adjustment too.

Discuss a wish to be alone together with calling arrangements and observation needed for safety. Whether the door closes or staff leave depends on wishes and assessed risks. A teaching picture of a worker leaving is not an instruction to leave everyone alone.

Check that the commode’s position, seat, stability and necessary supports suit the person. After use, support cleanliness, clothing, hand hygiene, odor and equipment management, through to returning to a safe place.

For a bedpan, prepare supplies, screening, body covering and a waterproof sheet, and check a planned posture and workable height. Ask the person to raise their hips only if possible and permitted. Check that the bedpan is correctly positioned, stable and not pressing on skin. The source illustrates someone able to bend their knees and raise their hips while clothing is lowered and the pan inserted. Align the anus with the receiving area and cover the body to limit exposure. Do not demand hip lifting or knee movement from someone who finds it difficult; use a trained method permitted for that individual.

The source example of raising the backrest for bedpan use explains its relationship to a posture that makes applying abdominal pressure easier. It does not instruct everyone to strain hard; actual backrest elevation follows condition and plan. Urinals have different shapes. The source illustrates side-lying with pillow support behind the back and using paper or similar material to direct urine into the urinal. Check a trained method suited to the body, ability to change posture and actual product, including position, leakage or splashing and skin contact. A gender label alone does not establish that one shape must fit.

After use, clean according to facility methods and remove the bedpan in a way suited to the person. The source illustrates asking someone able to lift their hips to do so for removal, observing skin, then turning them side-lying to remove the waterproof sheet. Confirm methods permitted for that individual before hip lifting or repositioning. Arrange clothing and bedding, return the bed to a safe height, and check condition and feelings before handling supplies. Removing the pan alone does not complete care.

For elimination assistance, select gloves, aprons and other protection according to anticipated contact with blood, body fluids or excreta and follow facility procedures. Gloves do not replace hand hygiene. Make necessary changes and perform hand hygiene when moving from dirty to clean work. The source includes a disposable apron example. Follow facility infection precautions and product instructions for use, replacement and disposal.

This learning organizes support purposes and checks. Follow individual plans and workplace training for transfers, repositioning and equipment operation. If you observe instability, pain, skin abnormalities or a change from usual condition, do not force the method to continue. Seek necessary help and report.

Learning case: when seated on the toilet, the call button is behind the person and out of reach. Check with them a position reachable and operable in the actual posture, rather than only checking that a button exists. Also review grab bars, the approach route, observation and privacy.

kaigo-atomic-clothing-seated.heading: Seated dressing and balance checks
paragraphs: First ask about condition and preferred clothes, explain the purpose and content of assistance and confirm consent. Provide screening and adjust room temperature. Describe shapes and features to someone with limited sight and, if wanted, let them check the fabric by touch.

The hemiplegia dressing example uses the unaffected side first when undressing and the affected side first when dressing. Removing the easier-moving side first reduces the burden of large movements on the weaker side. However, memorizing the order does not justify ignoring individual pain or movement restrictions.

Check sitting stability and which direction the person tends to lose balance. In the source’s seated hemiplegia dressing example, difficulty using strength on the affected side makes falling toward it more likely, so the worker supports from that side. Choose actual support from individual assessment; do not apply this position to every posture or person. Help where reaching or passing a sleeve is difficult rather than strongly pulling the shoulder or affected arm.

Lifting a foot during a trouser change may upset balance. If standing is possible and permitted, use reliable support. For unstable standing, the source also illustrates the seated person raising the unaffected hip and lowering the trousers as far as possible. Check whether this action is possible and permitted. Do not force hip lifting, leg lifting or standing on someone who is leaning. If difficult, review support and method and choose assistance consistent with the plan.

The trouser-dressing example also inserts the affected leg first, followed by the unaffected leg. Pull them up as far as possible while seated, then adjust while standing only if necessary and safe. Do not confuse ‘unaffected side first off, affected side first on’ with an instruction that the person must stand.

Afterward, check underwear and fabric wrinkles, displacement, comfort, pain, skin and condition. Clothing merely being on the body does not establish safe, comfortable dressing. Actual methods follow the person’s plan and training.

Learning case: while changing trousers, the worker asks the person to lift a foot even though their sitting posture is leaning. Stop the destabilizing method, check condition, support and possible postures, and request necessary assistance.

kaigo-atomic-clothing-bed.heading: Dressing in bed and checks afterward
paragraphs: For dressing in bed with hemiplegia too, check what the person can do and use the unaffected-side-first-off, affected-side-first-on principle. Before starting, arrange condition checks, explanation and consent, room temperature, screening and clothing choice.

In the upper-garment removal example, remove the unaffected sleeve first and gather the removed fabric inward. Use safe repositioning suited to the person when moving clothing from beneath the body. Do not forcibly pull the body or affected shoulder to extract fabric.

The textbook illustrates turning onto the unaffected side, removing clothing from behind the back, then removing the affected sleeve. That direction does not suit every illness or injury. Check permitted posture, shoulder protection and necessary staffing or equipment based on assessment and training.

In the dressing example, put the affected sleeve on first, arrange the garment body, spread the back using planned repositioning, and then put on the unaffected sleeve. Check the back and side seams, wrinkles and twists. Getting the garment on and checking comfort are separate outcomes.

The trouser example also removes from the unaffected side first and dresses the affected side first. Even if hip lifting is illustrated for someone able to do it, do not demand it from everyone. Check whether it is possible and permitted; otherwise use an individual assistance method.

The helper’s position need not be identical for seated and in-bed dressing examples. In the lying upper-garment example, the worker approaches from the unaffected side to handle buttons and gather clothing. The example protecting seated stability has different conditions. Do not mechanically apply one position to every action.

Afterward, ask how the person feels and check pain, skin, clothing position, wrinkles and condition. Correct twisted seams using a safe posture. Do not leave discomfort unresolved merely because the appearance or dressing action seems complete.
Learning case: putting on the top is complete, but the back seam is twisted. Adjust it in a safe posture and check pain, comfort and skin. Do not conclude ‘clothes on, care finished.’

kaigo-atomic-face-hair-makeup.heading: Support face washing, hair care and makeup through personal choice
paragraphs: Face washing removes skin dirt and can help start the day pleasantly. If independent washing is difficult, check wishes and condition and use a suitable towel or other items to help where needed.

Even with a warm towel, check its heat and the person’s tolerance. Removing dirt and moisturizing to prevent dryness serve different purposes. Use methods and products suited to skin condition rather than choosing the same for everyone.

Ask about hairstyle preferences and arrange hair after checking hair and scalp condition. Even someone who cannot easily raise their arms may retain independent parts with a comb whose handle and shape fit. Do not finish merely by handing over equipment: check posture and ease of use.

The source explains that scalp brushing removes dirt and that appropriate stimulation promotes circulation. This does not mean stronger stimulation or continuous rubbing is better. Avoid pain and skin strain, and discuss the desired style and necessary assistance. A request to arrange hair does not authorize an unwanted hairstyle change.

Makeup is one option for expressing individuality. Support those who want it without imposing it on those who do not. Before bed, help remove makeup using a skin-appropriate method while preserving what the person can do.

This explanation teaches personal choice and checks. Review methods if there are skin abnormalities or pain and consult the necessary responsible person. It does not instruct choosing cosmetics or moisturizers as substitutes for treatment of skin disease.

Learning case: the person wants to comb their own hair but cannot easily raise their arms high. Check the preferred style and scalp condition, adjust equipment and posture, and discuss a method in which they do the parts they can and receive help with difficult parts.

127.title: Support conversation according to communication needs
objectives: Choose communication methods suited to sight, hearing, understanding and expression.
Distinguish small verbal mistakes from information that requires checking for safety.
127.context: Learning case: the person uses the wrong name for an item but points to what they want to use. Rather than making them wait until they say the name correctly, check the indicated item and their wishes. However, do not omit checks when safety-related use is unclear.
127.artCaption: A scene using pictures and pointing to check together what the person wants to convey.

128.title: Check the recipient’s understanding in records and handovers
objectives: Record subjective and objective information, sources and event times separately.
Have recipients repeat key points and distinguish taking responsibility from completing tasks.
128.context: Learning case: the recipient remains silent after a report containing several times. Ask them to repeat key times, the person concerned, next actions and unconfirmed matters to check shared understanding. Do not record silence as agreement.
128.artCaption: Workers hand over information. The recipient also checks key points and who is responsible next.

129.title: Distinguish elimination aids and mechanisms of urinary leakage
objectives: Distinguish equipment purposes and different urinary-incontinence mechanisms.
Connect constipation and diarrhea support with the individual plan, observation and reporting.
129.context: Learning case: the person felt the urge to urinate but could not find the toilet in time. Do not finish with changing the brief alone. Check guidance, mobility assistance, timing, skin and wishes. Leakage alone does not diagnose the cause.
129.artCaption: A scene considering purposes of elimination aids and conditions suited to the person. The picture alone is not a procedure for selecting or positioning equipment.

130.title: Support each elimination stage and a usable environment
objectives: Identify assistance needed at each elimination stage.
Check calling, grab bars, privacy and cleanliness under actual conditions of use.
130.context: Learning case: when seated on the toilet, the call button is behind the person and out of reach. Check with them a position reachable and operable in the actual posture, rather than only checking that a button exists. Also review grab bars, the approach route, observation and privacy.
130.artCaption: A scene checking the toilet environment. Also check whether grab bars and the call system are usable in the person’s actual posture.

131.title: Seated dressing and balance checks
objectives: Confirm clothing choices and consent to assistance.
Check sitting stability and comfort rather than relying on dressing order alone.
131.context: Learning case: while changing trousers, the worker asks the person to lift a foot even though their sitting posture is leaning. Stop the destabilizing method, check condition, support and possible postures, and request necessary assistance.
131.artCaption: The person chooses clothes they want to wear. Needing assistance does not mean staff also take over clothing choices.

132.title: Dressing in bed and checks afterward
objectives: Distinguish the in-bed dressing example from individual posture conditions.
Finish by checking twisted seams, pain, skin and comfort.
132.context: Learning case: putting on the top is complete, but the back seam is twisted. Adjust it in a safe posture and check pain, comfort and skin. Do not conclude ‘clothes on, care finished.’
132.artCaption: A scene asking about wishes near the bed. It does not illustrate technical steps for changing clothes while lying down.

133.title: Support face washing, hair care and makeup through personal choice
objectives: Respect the person’s hairstyle and makeup wishes.
Adjust equipment and posture to use the parts the person can do.
133.context: Learning case: the person wants to comb their own hair but cannot easily raise their arms high. Check the preferred style and scalp condition, adjust equipment and posture, and discuss a method in which they do the parts they can and receive help with difficult parts.
133.artCaption: A scene supporting the person’s own choices and actions they can perform. It is not a diagram of face washing, hair care or cosmetic use.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-accessible-talk.prompt: The person uses the wrong name for an item but points to what they want. What is appropriate?
options: Do not check wishes or help until they can say the correct name.
Check the indicated item and wishes, clarify safety-related uncertainties and connect them with necessary support.
Conclude that all understanding of explanations is lost because pronunciation is incorrect.
Treat use and wishes as confirmed merely by looking at the indicated item.
rationales: This makes correction of a small verbal mistake a condition for expressing wishes.
This respects intended meaning without filling gaps in safety information by assumption.
Difficulty with pronunciation or expression alone does not establish the degree of understanding.
Identifying an item does not establish its intended use or safety conditions.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-record-handover.prompt: The recipient remains silent after a handover containing several times. How can understanding be checked?
options: Ask the recipient to repeat key times, the person concerned, the next response and unconfirmed matters, and check for misunderstandings.
Record full understanding and a completed response because there was no objection.
Remove all times from records because they are complicated.
Accept no questions because the information has already been sent once.
rationales: Rather than only repeating the sender’s explanation, ask the recipient to repeat its content to check understanding. Silence is not evidence of understanding or acceptance of responsibility.
Understanding, accepting responsibility and completing action each require confirmation.
Removing times prevents communication of the course of events and deadlines for next actions.
Uncertainties need two-way checking; sending information once is insufficient.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-continence-type.prompt: The person felt the urge to urinate but could not find the toilet in time. Which support is appropriate?
options: Once leakage occurs, there is no need to check urges or mobility difficulties.
Changing the brief removes the need to check skin or personal wishes.
Check causes, environment, guidance and assistance timing while protecting initiative, skin and privacy.
Decide that all urinary leakage has the same mechanism.
rationales: Because the person feels the urge, also check factors such as location and movement that prevented timely arrival.
Changing alone does not establish skin condition or the elimination method the person wants.
Even with an urge, location or movement difficulties may prevent timely arrival. Managing leakage alone is insufficient.
Distinguish mechanisms involving abdominal pressure, strong urges, retained urine, nerves and daily actions.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-toilet-environm.prompt: When seated on the toilet, the person cannot reach the call button behind them. What should be checked?
options: If a button is installed, finish without reviewing its position.
Check a reachable, operable position in the actual seated posture, and review grab bars, approach and privacy.
Keep the door permanently open without asking wishes because they cannot call.
Treat the call system as unnecessary if a grab bar is present.
rationales: Installation alone does not establish that the person can request help.
Checking in actual use helps create an environment where necessary assistance can be requested.
Adjust privacy and safety together, considering wishes and observation needs.
A grab bar supports posture; its role differs from a call system requesting help.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-clothing-seated.prompt: During a trouser change, the worker asks the person to lift a foot even though their sitting posture is leaning. What needs review?
options: If the undressing sequence is correct, omit balance checks.
Continuing an unstable posture is acceptable if dressing finishes quickly.
Assume everyone can lift a foot while seated.
Stop the destabilizing method, check condition, support and possible postures, and preserve choice and privacy.
rationales: The unaffected/affected-side sequence alone does not guarantee sitting stability.
Saving time does not justify continuing a method that could lead to a fall.
Lifting a foot can upset balance even while seated. Check ability and support.
This adjusts the method to individual abilities rather than converting a sequence into an instruction that the person must stand.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-clothing-bed.prompt: Putting on the top is complete, but the back seam is twisted. What is appropriate?
options: Do not check comfort if the arms are through the sleeves.
Treat unseen back seams as irrelevant to the person.
Correct the twist in a safe posture and check skin, pain and comfort with the person.
Pull the fabric hard without checking posture or pain.
rationales: Completion of the action alone does not establish pain or skin strain.
Twists and wrinkles at the back may also cause discomfort or strain on skin.
This checks getting dressed separately from achieving a safe, comfortable fit.
Adjusting fabric also requires checking safe posture and strain on the body.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-face-hair-makeu.prompt: The person wants to comb their hair but cannot easily raise their arms high. What support is appropriate?
options: Check the preferred hairstyle and scalp, discuss suitable equipment or posture and enable the person to do the parts they can.
Take over hairstyle choices because raising an arm is difficult.
After handing over a comb, do not check whether it can actually be used.
Rub the scalp hard to improve circulation even if it hurts.
rationales: Rather than taking over everything, equipment and posture can use the person’s abilities while assistance covers difficult parts.
Needing movement assistance does not remove the right to choose.
Having equipment does not establish that it suits posture and abilities or can be used.
Avoid pain and skin strain rather than making stronger stimulation the goal.
